label: def:weighted_dlra
title: Definition
head: environment
name: WDLRA

title: Proposition
body_md:
Suppose that $\mathcal{Z}=USV^\top\in\mathcal{M}_r$ satisfies \Cref{def:weighted_dlra}, with initial data
\[
\mathcal{Z}(0)=U^0S^0(V^0)^\top\in\mathcal{M}_r,
\qquad
(U^0)^\top M_xU^0=I_r,
\qquad
(V^0)^\top M_yV^0=I_r.
\]
Then, WDLRA \eqref{eq:weighted_dlra_dr} is equivalent to the following formulations:
\begin{enumerate}
\par\hangindent 40\p@[(i)] \textbf{Galerkin formulation.}
Find $\partial_t\mathcal{Z}\in T_{\mathcal{Z}}\mathcal{M}_r$ such that
\begin{align*}
(\partial_t\mathcal{Z}-\mathscr{L}(\mathcal{Z}),\delta Z)_M=0,
\qquad
\forall\,\delta Z\in T_{\mathcal{Z}}\mathcal{M}_r,
\end{align*}
with the initial condition $\mathcal{Z}(0)=U^0S^0(V^0)^\top$.

\par\hangindent 40\p@[(ii)] \textbf{Equations of motion.}
The factors $U$, $S$, and $V$ satisfy
\begin{align*}
\dot U
&=P_U^\perp M_x\mathscr{L}(\mathcal{Z})M_yVS^{-1},
&
\dot S
&=U^\top M_x\mathscr{L}(\mathcal{Z})M_yV,
\\
\dot V
&=P_V^\perp M_y\mathscr{L}(\mathcal{Z})^\top M_xUS^{-\top},
\end{align*}
with initial conditions
$U(0) = U^0$, $S(0) = S^0$, $V(0) = V^0$.

\par\hangindent 40\p@[(iii)] \textbf{KLS system.}
Let $K=US$ and $L=VS^\top$. Then $K$, $L$, and $S$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{KLS}
    \begin{aligned}
        \dot K
&=\mathscr{L}(KV^\top)M_yV,
\quad 
\dot L
=\mathscr{L}(UL^\top)^\top M_xU,
\\
\dot S
&=U^\top M_x\mathscr{L}(USV^\top)M_yV,
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
with initial conditions
 $K(0) = U^0 S^0$, $L(0) = V^0 (S^0)^\top$, $S(0) = S^0$.
\end{enumerate}

label: thm:wp32
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Well-posedness

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) We present the proof for the $S$-step in detail; the $K$- and $L$-steps follow by the same reasoning. Since \eqref{eq:Svar32} is a finite-dimensional linear system, existence is equivalent to uniqueness. Thus, it suffices to prove uniqueness.

Suppose that $w_{S,1}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}$ and $w_{S,2}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}$ are two solutions of \eqref{eq:Svar32} corresponding to the same data $\hat w_h^\mathfrak{n}$. Define
\(
\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}
:=w_{S,1}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}-w_{S,2}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}
\in V_0^{\mathfrak{n}+1}.
\)
Subtracting the two equations gives
\[
\bigl(D_t\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1},w_0\bigr)_h
+A(\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1},w_0)
=\alpha\bigl(\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1},w_0\bigr)_h,
\quad
\forall\,w_0\in V_0^{\mathfrak{n}+1}.
\]
Since both solutions share the same previous-time data, 
\(
\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}}=0,
\)
and hence
\[
D_t\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}
=\frac{\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}}{\Delta t}.
\]
Taking $w_0=\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}$ yields
\[
\frac{1}{\Delta t}
\|\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2
+\|\nabla\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
=
\alpha\|\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2,
\]
where we have used
\(
A(v,v)=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.
\)
Therefore,
\[
\left(\frac{1}{\Delta t}-\alpha\right)
\|\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2
+\|\nabla\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
=0.
\]
Since $\Delta t>0$ and $\alpha\le0$, we have
\(
\frac{1}{\Delta t}-\alpha>0.
\)
Both terms in the above identity are therefore nonnegative, which implies
\(
\|\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h=0.
\)
Hence,
\(
\delta w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}=0,
\)
and consequently
\[
w_{S,1}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}=w_{S,2}^{\mathfrak{n}+1}.
\]
Thus, the $S$-step solution is unique.

The existence and uniqueness of the solution
$(K^{\mathfrak{n}+1},L^{\mathfrak{n}+1},S^{\mathfrak{n}+1})$
in \Cref{alg:KLS-Steps} then follow from those of \eqref{wkls} and \Cref{lem:mateqfem}.

(ii) Choose $w_0 = w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}$ in \eqref{eq:Svar32} to obtain
\[
  \bigl(D_t w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}, w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\bigr)_h
  + \|\nabla w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
  = \alpha\|w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2.
\]
Applying the polarization identity
\(
  (a-b,a)
  = \frac{1}{2}
  \left(
    \|a\|^2-\|b\|^2+\|a-b\|^2
  \right)
\)
with $a=w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}$ and $b=w_S^\mathfrak{n}$, and multiplying by $2\Delta t$, gives
\[
  \|w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2
  -\|w_S^\mathfrak{n}\|_h^2
  +\|w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}-w_S^\mathfrak{n}\|_h^2
  +2\Delta t
  \|\nabla w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2
  =
  2\Delta t\,\alpha
  \|w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2.
\]
Since $\Delta t>0$ and $\alpha\leq0$, the right-hand side is nonpositive, while the third and fourth terms on the left-hand side are nonnegative. Hence,
\[
  \|w_S^{\mathfrak{n}+1}\|_h^2
  \leq
  \|w_S^\mathfrak{n}\|_h^2.
\]
By \Cref{def:lows}, this is equivalent to \eqref{l2stab}.

label: lem:psd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:psd}
Let $A_x$ and $A_y$ denote the stiffness matrices associated with the
one-dimensional periodic finite element discretizations in the
$x$- and $y$-directions, respectively. Then, the following results hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \par\hangindent 40\p@[(i)] $A_x$ and $A_y$ are positive semidefinite, namely,
    \[
        A_x\succeq0,
        \qquad
        A_y\succeq0.
    \]
    
    \par\hangindent 40\p@[(ii)]
    Let $\widehat{A}_x$ and $\widehat{A}_y$ denote the
    $(2k+1)$-banded parts of $A_x$ and $A_y$, respectively, obtained by
    retaining only the entries within the $(2k+1)$ banded diagonals.
    Then, $\widehat{A}_x$ and $\widehat{A}_y$ are also positive semidefinite, namely,
    \[
        \widehat{A}_x\succeq0,
        \qquad
        \widehat{A}_y\succeq0.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove the assertions for $A_x$ and $\widehat{A}_x$;
the arguments for $A_y$ and $\widehat{A}_y$ are analogous.

{(i)}
Let $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^m$ be arbitrary, and let
$v_h$ be the corresponding finite element function,
\(
    v_h(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_j\phi_j(x),
\)
where $\{\phi_j\}_{j=1}^m$ denotes the finite element basis.
By the definition of the stiffness matrix,
\begin{equation}
    v^\top A_x v
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^{M}
    \int_{I_i^x}
    \left(v_h'(x)\right)^2\,dx
    \ge 0.
\end{equation}
Hence,
\[
    A_x\succeq0.
\]

{(ii)}
For each element $I_i^x$, let
\[
    K^{(i)}
    =
    \left[
        \int_{I_i^x}
        \phi_{(i-1)k+p}'(x)
        \phi_{(i-1)k+q}'(x)\,dx
    \right]_{p,q=1}^{k+1}
    \in\mathbb{R}^{(k+1)\times(k+1)}
\]
denote the corresponding local stiffness matrix. For any
$z=(z_1,\ldots,z_{k+1})^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{k+1}$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
    z^\top K^{(i)}z
    &=
    \int_{I_i^x}
    \left(
        \sum_{p=1}^{k+1}
        z_p\phi_{(i-1)k+p}'(x)
    \right)^2\,dx
    \ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus,
\[
    K^{(i)}\succeq0,
    \qquad i=1,\ldots,M.
\]

For $i=1,\ldots,M-1$, the standard finite element assembly gives
\[
    R_i^\top K^{(i)}R_i,
\]
where $R_i \in \mathbb{R}^{(k+1)\times m}$ denotes the local-to-global restriction matrix.

For the last element $I_M^x$, the periodic identification of the
endpoints causes the last local degree of freedom to coincide with
the first global degree of freedom. Consequently, the corresponding
entries coupling these two sets of degrees of freedom appear in the
corner blocks of $A_x$ and lie outside the $(2k+1)$ banded diagonals.
Removing these entries amounts to replacing $K^{(M)}$ by
\[
    \widehat{K}^{(M)}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        K^{(M)}_{1:k,1:k} & 0\\
        0 & K^{(M)}_{k+1,k+1}
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since $K^{(M)}\succeq0$, its principal submatrix satisfies
\[
    K^{(M)}_{1:k,1:k}\succeq0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    K^{(M)}_{k+1,k+1}
    =
    \int_{I_M^x}
    \left|\phi_m'(x)\right|^2\,dx
    \ge0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
    \widehat{K}^{(M)}\succeq0.
\]

It follows that the $(2k+1)$-banded part of $A_x$ admits the
decomposition
\[
    \widehat{A}_x
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^{M-1}
    R_i^\top K^{(i)}R_i
    +
    R_M^\top\widehat{K}^{(M)}R_M,
\]
where $R_M$ denotes the local-to-global restriction matrix without
the periodic wrap-around contribution.

Therefore, for any $v\in\mathbb{R}^m$,
\begin{align}
    v^\top\widehat{A}_xv
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^{M-1}
    (R_iv)^\top K^{(i)}(R_iv)
    +
    (R_Mv)^\top
    \widehat{K}^{(M)}
    (R_Mv)
    \ge0.
\end{align}
Hence,
\[
    \widehat{A}_x\succeq0.
\]
The proof is complete.

label: Ajnons
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Recall that
\[
    A=-\Delta t\,L_x
    =\Delta t\,M_x^{-1}A_x
    \qquad\text{or}\qquad
    A=-\Delta t\,L_y
    =\Delta t\,M_y^{-1}A_y.
\]
Let $\widehat{A}_x$ and $\widehat{A}_y$ be the matrices defined in
\Cref{lem:psd}. Then, for the matrix $\widehat{A}$ defined in
\eqref{eq:A-periodic-structure}, we have
\[
    \widehat{A}
    =\Delta t\,M_x^{-1}\widehat{A}_x
    \qquad\text{or}\qquad
    \widehat{A}
    =\Delta t\,M_y^{-1}\widehat{A}_y.
\]
Since $M_x\succ0$ and $\widehat{A}_x\succeq0$ by
\Cref{lem:psd},
\[
    M_x^{-1}\widehat{A}_x
    \sim
    M_x^{-1/2}\widehat{A}_xM_x^{-1/2}
    \succeq0.
\]
Hence, all eigenvalues of $\widehat{A}$ are real and nonnegative.
The same conclusion follows when
\[
    \widehat{A}
    =\Delta t\,M_y^{-1}\widehat{A}_y.
\]

Moreover, since $\alpha\leq0$ and $A_y\succeq0$ by
\Cref{lem:psd}, we have
\[
    B
    =(1-\Delta t\,\alpha)I_r
      +\Delta t\,(V^\mathfrak{n})^\top A_yV^\mathfrak{n}
    \succ0.
\]
Therefore, all eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of $B$ satisfy
\[
    \lambda_j>0,
    \qquad j=1,\ldots,r.
\]

By \eqref{eq:shifted-periodic-decomp}, each $\widehat{A}_j$ is a
positive shift of $\widehat{A}$, namely,
\[
    \widehat{A}_j=\widehat{A}+\lambda_j I.
\]
Thus, if $\mu$ is any eigenvalue of $\widehat{A}$, then
$\mu\geq0$, and the corresponding eigenvalue of $\widehat{A}_j$ is
\[
    \mu+\lambda_j>0.
\]
Hence, $\widehat{A}_j$ is nonsingular for every $j=1,\ldots,r$.

Finally, by \eqref{eq:shifted-periodic-decomp},
\[
    \widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
    =A+\lambda_j I.
\]
Since $M_x\succ0$ and $A_x\succeq0$ by \Cref{lem:psd},
\[
    M_x^{-1}A_x
    \sim
    M_x^{-1/2}A_xM_x^{-1/2}
    \succeq0.
\]
Therefore, all eigenvalues of $A$ are real and nonnegative. The same
conclusion follows from
\[
    A=\Delta t\,M_y^{-1}A_y
\]
using $M_y\succ0$ and $A_y\succeq0$. Consequently, all eigenvalues of
\[
    A+\lambda_j I
    =\widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
\]
are strictly positive, since $\lambda_j>0$. Hence,
$\widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}$ is nonsingular for every
$j=1,\ldots,r$.

(ii)
By (i), both $\widehat{A}_j$ and
$\widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}$ are nonsingular. Since
$\widehat{A}_j$ is nonsingular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det\left(
    \widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
\right)
&=
            
                   
            
                                
                                       
             
           
\det(\widehat{A}_j)
\det\left(
    I_m+\widehat{A}_j^{-1}
    \widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
By Sylvester's determinant theorem,
\[
\det(I_m+XY)=\det(I_2+YX),
\]
with
\[
X=\widehat{A}_j^{-1}\widehat{U}
\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times2},
\qquad
Y=\widehat{V}^{\top}
\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times m}.
\]
Hence,
\[
\det\left(
    I_m+\widehat{A}_j^{-1}
    \widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
\right)
=
\det\left(
    I_2+\widehat{V}^{\top}
    \widehat{A}_j^{-1}\widehat{U}
\right).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\det\left(
    \widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}
\right)
=
\det(\widehat{A}_j)
\det\left(
    I_2+\widehat{V}^{\top}
    \widehat{A}_j^{-1}\widehat{U}
\right).
\]
By (i), the determinants of
$\widehat{A}_j$ and
$\widehat{A}_j+\widehat{U}\widehat{V}^{\top}$ are both nonzero.
Therefore,
\[
    \det\left(
        I_2+\widehat{V}^{\top}
        \widehat{A}_j^{-1}\widehat{U}
    \right)\neq0.
\]
Thus, the conclusion (ii) holds.

label: ex:accuracy
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:accuracy}
In this example, we assess the spatial and temporal convergence
properties of the FR-MLFEM and BUG-MLFEM schemes.


                                                                                  
                                 
                                                                                  

We first investigate the spatial convergence of the FR-MLFEM and
BUG-MLFEM schemes. The spatial
discretization uses $P_k$ finite elements with $k=1,2,3$, and the
error is measured in the mass-lumped $L^2(\Omega)$ norm at the final time
$T=0.1$.
                  
         
       
             
                                 
                             
                         
                
For the spatial convergence tests, we take the default time step size. 
                                                                                                       
The spatial convergence results are presented in
\Cref{fig:spatial_accuracy_all_bcs}. For both FR-MLFEM and BUG-MLFEM,
the numerical errors decrease at the optimal rate $k+1$ for the
$P_k$ finite element approximations. More importantly, the optimal
spatial convergence behavior is consistently maintained for all three
types of boundary conditions.
The BUG-MLFEM scheme exhibits the same asymptotic convergence rates as
the corresponding FR-MLFEM scheme. This agreement confirms that the
low-rank dynamical formulation does not degrade the spatial accuracy
of the underlying finite element discretization.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering

                       
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_01.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_02.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_03.png}

    \vspace{0.1cm}

                           
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_04.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_05.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.315\textwidth]{graphs/photo_06.png}

    \caption{Spatial convergence of the FR-MLFEM (top row) and
BUG-MLFEM (bottom row) schemes using $P_k$ elements with
$k=1,2,3$ at $T=0.1$. From left to right, the columns correspond to
homogeneous Dirichlet, homogeneous Neumann, and periodic boundary
conditions.}
    \label{fig:spatial_accuracy_all_bcs}
\end{figure}


                                                                                  
                                  
                                                                                  

We next investigate the temporal convergence of the FR-MLFEM and
BUG-MLFEM schemes. We
fix the spatial mesh sufficiently fine and use $P_2$ finite
elements. 
        
                                                  
  
              
                        
                        
                         
                       
                         
                                               
   
The error is again
measured in the mass-lumped $L^2(\Omega)$ norm at the final time.
The temporal convergence results are shown in
\Cref{fig:temporal_convergence}. Both FR-MLFEM and BUG-MLFEM exhibit
the expected first-order temporal convergence. The same first-order
behavior is observed for all three types of boundary conditions,
confirming that the low-rank formulation preserves the temporal
accuracy of the underlying first-order time integrator.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.32\textwidth]{graphs/photo_07.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.32\textwidth]{graphs/photo_08.png}
    \hfill
    \includegraphics[width=0.32\textwidth]{graphs/photo_09.png}
    \caption{Temporal convergence of the FR-MLFEM and BUG-MLFEM schemes for $P_2$ polynomials. From left to right: homogeneous Dirichlet, homogeneous Neumann, and periodic BCs.}
    \label{fig:temporal_convergence}
\end{figure}

name: Accuracy and convergence tests

title: Example
body_md:
We continue the test cases above to compare the computational costs of the FR-MLFEM and BUG-MLFEM schemes using the different approaches described in \Cref{sec:cost}. All tests employ $P_2$ finite elements, the default time step, and a final time of $T=0.01$.
The CPU-time results in \Cref{tab:cpu_all_bc} demonstrate the substantial computational advantage of Approach~III over Approaches~I and~II for all three boundary conditions. For the relatively coarse mesh ($N=40$), Approach~III reduces the CPU time from $74.93$--$126.57$ seconds for Approach~I to $8.14$--$22.70$ seconds, achieving speedups ranging from $5.58\times$ to $9.21\times$. In comparison, Approach~II provides only modest improvements, with speedups of $1.06\times$--$1.12\times$. As the mesh is refined to $N=80$, the computational advantage of Approach~III becomes more pronounced. While Approaches~I and~II require approximately $6.9\times10^3$--$1.2\times10^4$ seconds, Approach~III completes the computations in $178.03$--$471.14$ seconds, yielding speedups of $25.49\times$--$38.80\times$. The advantage is even more significant for the finest mesh, $N=160$, where Approaches~I and~II require approximately $2.1\times10^5$--$3.6\times10^5$ seconds, whereas Approach~III requires only $2838.81$--$6576.58$ seconds. The resulting speedups reach $54.35\times$--$81.38\times$, with the largest gain observed for homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. These results demonstrate that the computational savings of the proposed Approach~III increase substantially with mesh refinement, whereas Approach~II offers only limited improvements over Approach~I. The speedup for periodic boundary conditions is comparatively smaller than those for homogeneous Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions on the finer meshes, which is consistent with the additional low-rank correction required to account for the periodic wrap-around entries in \Cref{alg:sylvester-periodic}.

title: Example
body_md:
To further examine the computational cost of the proposed Sylvester
solvers, we investigate the dependence of the CPU time, excluding the initial GSVD of $W^0$, on the spatial grid size $N$ and rank $r$. 
Here, the spatial discretization is based on the \(P_1\) polynomials.
First, we fix $r=2$ and increase $N$ from
$10$ to $320$, with the results reported in
\Cref{tab:cpu_time_N_r2}. For all three types of boundary conditions, the
CPU time remains nearly unchanged for small $N$, where the fixed
computational overhead is dominant. As $N$ increases, the CPU time grows
more rapidly, and the observed scaling rates approach or exceed one at
the finest mesh. In particular, at $N=320$, the CPU times are $97.73$,
$87.12$, and $119.48$ seconds for the Dirichlet, Neumann, and Periodic
BCs, respectively. The results demonstrate that the
computational cost exhibits approximately linear growth with respect to
$N$ in the practically relevant large-$N$ regime, consistent with the
linear dependence on the number of spatial degrees of freedom in the
proposed solver.

Next, we fix $N=320$ and vary the rank from $r=1$ to $r=10$, as shown in
\Cref{tab:cpu_time_r_N320}. The CPU time increases steadily with $r$ for
all three boundary conditions. For example, for the Dirichlet case, the
CPU time increases from $76.53$ seconds at $r=1$ to $204.42$ seconds at
$r=10$, while the corresponding increase is from $72.39$ to
$200.87$ seconds for the Neumann case. The periodic case requires
additional computational work due to the low-rank correction in
\Cref{alg:sylvester-periodic}, resulting in consistently higher CPU
time. The observed scaling rates with respect to $r$ remain below the
quadratic rate associated with the $O((m+n)r^2)$ complexity. This
is consistent with the overall complexity of the proposed solver, which
also contains lower-order terms in $r$ and rank-independent operations.
Consequently, the measured CPU time grows more slowly than quadratically
over the tested range of $r$.

title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:augbug}

Following \cite{ceruti2024robust}, we assess the accuracy, computational
efficiency, and rank adaptivity of the augmented BUG integrator
\Cref{alg:AugBUG-Steps} for a stiff, forced heat equation on the two-dimensional
torus $\Omega=[-\pi,\pi)^2$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stiff_heat}
  \partial_t u(x,y,t)
  = \frac{1}{2}\left(
      \partial_{xx}u(x,y,t)+\partial_{yy}u(x,y,t)
    \right)+g(x,y),
\end{equation}
subject to periodic boundary conditions in both spatial directions. The
time-independent forcing term and the initial condition are, respectively, given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stiff_forcing}
  g(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{11}10^{-(j-1)}
  \exp\!\bigl(-j(x^2+y^2)\bigr)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stiff_ic}
  u(x,y,0)=\sin(x)\sin(y).
\end{equation}

We first examine spatial convergence. We fix the time step at
$\Delta t=10^{-5}$ and set the initial rank to $r^0=10$. For polynomial
degrees $k=1,2,3$, we refine the spatial mesh and measure the $L^2(\Omega)$
error at $T=1$. Since the exact solution is unavailable, we
use the FR-MLFEM solution on a fine mesh with $N=160$ as the reference
solution. The results are presented in \Cref{fig:stiff_heat_space}.
Both FR-MLFEM and augmented BUG-MLFEM (ABUG-MLFEM) exhibit the optimal spatial convergence
rate $k+1$. Moreover, their error curves are nearly indistinguishable,
suggesting that the low-rank approximation
introduces no discernible error beyond that associated with spatial
discretization.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}[b]{0.45\textwidth}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{graphs/photo_10.png}
    \label{fig:stiff_heat_space_FR}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}[b]{0.45\textwidth}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{graphs/photo_11.png}
    \label{fig:stiff_heat_space_BUG}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Spatial convergence at $T=1$ for polynomial degrees
$k=1,2,3$, with $\Delta t=10^{-5}$ and initial rank $r^0=10$.
Left: FR-MLFEM; right: ABUG-MLFEM.
                                                     
  }
  \label{fig:stiff_heat_space}
\end{figure}

We next compare the computational costs of the two methods using the
approaches described in \Cref{sec:cost}. All runs employ $\mathbb{P}^2$
finite elements, $\Delta t=10^{-5}$, and final time $T=1$.
The measured CPU times and the speedups relative to Approach~I are reported
in \Cref{tab:cpu_stiff_heat}. Approach~III is the most efficient of the
three approaches at every mesh resolution. Its speedup increases from
$2.67\times$ for $N=40$ to $15.63\times$ for $N=80$ and
$38.09\times$ for $N=160$. In particular, for $N=160$, the CPU time
decreases from $24294.81$ seconds for Approach~I to $637.83$ seconds
for Approach~III. By comparison, Approach~II yields only modest speedups,
ranging from $1.02\times$ to $1.09\times$. These results demonstrate the
substantial computational advantage of Approach~III for this stiff test
problem, with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the mesh is refined.

We then investigate temporal convergence. We fix $N=80$, $k=2$, and
$r^0=10$, and successively halve the time step from
$\Delta t=10^{-2}$ to $\Delta t=6.25\times10^{-4}$. The $L^2(\Omega)$
error is evaluated at $T=1$. As shown in the left panel of
\Cref{fig:stiff_heat_time_rank}, both FR-MLFEM and ABUG-MLFEM
exhibit first-order convergence in time. Their errors are nearly identical
for all tested time steps, indicating that the augmented BUG integrator
preserves the temporal accuracy of the underlying time discretization in
these experiments.

Finally, we examine the rank evolution of ABUG-MLFEM for
polynomial degrees $k=1,2,3$ up to $T=2.5$, using $\Delta t=10^{-2}$
and truncation tolerance $\vartheta=10^{-12}$. The rank histories are shown
in the right panel of \Cref{fig:stiff_heat_time_rank}. Each term in
\eqref{eq:stiff_forcing} is separable, since
\(
  \exp\!\bigl(-j(x^2+y^2)\bigr)
  =\exp(-jx^2)\exp(-jy^2).
\)
Consequently, the forcing term has separation rank at most $11$.
The geometrically decreasing coefficients $10^{-(j-1)}$ produce modes
of progressively smaller amplitude. As these modes contribute to the
evolving solution, the adaptive integrator increases the rank in discrete
steps, from $8$ to $9$ and then to $10$. The rank subsequently remains
at $10$ over the simulated interval, with the remaining modes not retained
under the prescribed truncation tolerance. The rank histories are similar
for all three polynomial degrees, although the times at which the rank
increases differ: the $\mathbb{P}^2$ computation reaches rank $10$ at
approximately $t=0.2$, whereas the $\mathbb{P}^1$ and $\mathbb{P}^3$
computations reach this rank at approximately $t=0.6$. This behavior
suggests that the adaptive rank is primarily determined by the effective
low-rank structure of the evolving solution, while the spatial
discretization can affect the timing of rank enrichment.
